title: Playing tenor in the Savoy relief band for the first time
summary: Reynolds hired Carney and Holmes for a dinner-hour relief band; Carney took alto, leaving Holmes on Elmer Williams's tenor, which he had never played.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: The next day, down around the club, Chick was out there, and he was just braggin'... "Hey! Here he comes now." And I come down the street... "Here he comes now. This is the man outswung Johnny Hodges in the cuttin' contest last night." Well, Chick just spread my name all over. He said, "Them two boys from Boston, they are something else." Well, that was all right, appearing at the Savoy, because Harry was playing his instrument at the Savoy. I was on the tenor. I had never had a tenor in my hands before, and it was...
Well, who gave you the tenor?

It was a European tenor... It was Elmer Williams' tenor. Elmer was the tenor player with Chick's band. See, they wanted a relief band to play one hour up there, the dinner hour, you know... So Reynolds, Elbrook(?) Reynolds, he got the band. And he came around the Rhythm Club (not the Rhythm Club), the Band Box at that time to get some musicians. So somebody told him about Harry Carney and me being saxophonists. So he hired us right away. Yeah. He told us, 'Well, be at the Savoy tomorrow night at such-and-such a time.' And there we go.

Well, he wanted an alto and a tenor. So somebody decided who is going to play alto and who is going to play tenor between Harry and me. So Harry said, 'He plays the tenor, I'll play the alto.' I was wondering why he didn't let me play the alto. That's all I had ever played. You know, I didn't know nothin' about no tenor. Anyway, it was all right with me. Okay, I'll be congenial.

And I'm up there, and the tenor's as big as I am. And it's supposed to be that big, you know. I couldn't have been too bad, because in them days, when they wanted you to play a chorus or something, they'd tell you to 'get off' -- you know, solo. What do I know? I'm just here from the country. So we ended up there playing, and the leader says

"Get off!" And I get up, and I'm crawlin' off the stand. He said, "Come back here. Where you goin'?" I say, "You said 'Get off.'" He says, "I mean play. Play a chorus." I said, "Oh." And here I am with this big tenor, and I don't know, Lord, it was terrible to me.

But it couldn't have been too bad. They applauded. [LAUGHS] People were very gracious. They applauded when I got through. So I don't know if it waas good or bad. But anyway, the word got out about the two saxophone players, you know, from Boston, and the word went from one to another.
